title: Choice Doesn't Always Mean Agency
author: Helena Farrell
summary: Drawing on her research into learners' experience of Universal Design for Learning in further education, Farrell argues that offering choice is not the same as creating agency. Learners may avoid alternative assessment formats because they fear being marked down, so the choice exists on paper while agency does not exist in practice. She proposes that learners must understand the ask before they can choose the how, and she sets out a three-stage frame of the ask, the how and the evidence. Meaningful agency requires understanding, confidence, scaffolding and genuine voice. The move is to shift how UDL is judged, from the number of options provided to the quality of the learner experience.
points: Offering options is relatively easy, while creating the conditions for meaningful choice is considerably more complex.
Learners may fear that alternative formats will be marked down, so a written assignment still feels like the only safe route.
Learners need to understand the ask (the learning outcome) before they can meaningfully choose the how.
Agency requires understanding, confidence, scaffolding and a genuine voice, and autonomy and support are not opposites.
UDL should not be reduced to a checklist, and inclusion should be measured by quality of experience rather than number of options.
quotes: Are we giving learners choices, or are we creating the conditions for them to exercise agency?
The choice exists on paper. The agency may not exist in practice.
The value of an assessment should be determined by the learning it demonstrates, not by an unquestioned preference for the format in which it is presented.
Learners need to understand the ASK before they can meaningfully choose the HOW.

Agency does not mean leaving learners to figure everything out for themselves. Sometimes the most empowering thing an educator can do is provide structure, model an approach and build confidence before encouraging greater independence.
These questions move us away from measuring inclusion by the number of options we provide and towards considering the quality of the experience we create.
Don’t just give learners choices. Create the conditions that allow them to make meaningful choices.
